extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in constitutional law, comparative politics, and institutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative standards about judicial power, political jurisdiction, and federal/state division from a comparative analysis of American, French, and English constitutional practice (Tocqueville). Useful for analyzing constitutional design and institutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial right to base decisions on the constitution rather than laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have acknowledged the right of the judges to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws; they have left them at liberty not to apply such laws as may appear to them to be unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power gives American judges immense political influence. Tocqueville explains it as a foundational difference from France and England; it is legitimate in the U.S. because the constitution is the origin of authority and may be altered by the people in prescribed ways. The text warns of political consequences but treats the right as natural for magistrates to select the obligation by which they are most strictly bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional amendability as a safeguard against judicial usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: An American constitution is not supposed to be immutable...it may be altered by the will of the people in predetermined cases, according to established rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the people can change the constitution, judges who refuse to apply laws on constitutional grounds do not permanently usurp sovereign power. Tocqueville contrasts this with France (immutable constitution risks judges becoming the supreme power) and England (parliament-as-constituent), using amendability as a key legitimating safeguard for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial priority of the constitution over ordinary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the constitution governs the legislator as much as the private citizen; as it is the first of laws it cannot be modified by a law, and it is therefore just that the tribunals should obey the constitution in preference to any law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as both a political and logical necessity: magistrates naturally select the most binding legal obligation. The text frames this as proper judicial behavior within a constitutional order where the constitution is supreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channeling constitutional challenges through individual lawsuits rather than general censure
rubrics_metrics.description: By connecting the censorship of the laws with the private interests of members of the community, and by intimately uniting the prosecution of the law with the prosecution of an individual, legislation is protected from wanton assailants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that judges contest laws only when a law is applied in a particular case; this conceals the political importance of an attack and limits court-driven political agitation. It prevents judges from openly attacking legislators and reduces public party-driven conflict. Trade-off: some laws may never be litigated and thus escape review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of judicial review to concrete cases reduces politicization but creates gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The political question which he is called upon to resolve is connected with the interest of the suitors, and he cannot refuse to decide it without abdicating the duties of his post...the judicial censorship which is exercised by the courts of justice over the legislation cannot extend to all laws indiscriminately, inasmuch as some of them can never give rise to that exact species of contestation which is termed a lawsuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes this as an intended feature: concentrating challenges through ordinary suits diminishes the judge's public political role while leaving certain statutes unchecked; the remedy is incomplete by design to avoid judicial excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that laws be attacked through the courts alone limits judicial political activism
rubrics_metrics.description: The evils of this power are considerably diminished by the obligation which has been imposed of attacking the laws through the courts of justice alone. If the judge had been empowered to contest the laws on the ground of theoretical generalities, if he had been enabled to open an attack or to pass a censure on the legislator, he would have played a prominent part in the political sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville treats the procedural limitation (attack via adjudicated cases) as a central constraint protecting legislation from arbitrary judicial political action and from turning judges into public champions or antagonists of parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen right to indict public functionaries before ordinary tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: In a free country like America all the citizens should have the right of indicting public functionaries before the ordinary tribunals, and all the judges should have the power of punishing public offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville defends this as natural and effective: making public officers responsible to ordinary courts increases respect for authority and makes officials more cautious. He observes few political trials because suits are costly and require serious grounds, which curbs frivolous prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of minor prosecutions as a better pledge of freedom than rare impeachments
rubrics_metrics.description: They hold that the right of minor prosecutions, which are within the reach of the whole community, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions which are rarely employed until it is too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts decentralised, accessible legal actions (minor prosecutions) with centralized impeachment as more effective guarantees of liberty because they are usable by many citizens rather than only by high political actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for certainty and mildness of justice over severe, rare punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: When justice is more certain and more mild, it is at the same time more efficacious. The English and the Americans hold that tyranny and oppression are to be treated like any other crime, by lessening the penalty and facilitating conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative criterion recommends institutional designs that lower barriers to conviction and reduce extreme penalties to improve enforcement and deter abuse; historically contrasted with medieval harsh punishments that did not reduce crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction defined as a temporary legal decision-making right vested in a political body
rubrics_metrics.description: I understand, by political jurisdiction, that temporary right of pronouncing a legal decision with which a political body may be invested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a conceptual standard: political jurisdiction is special, time-bound authority given to political assemblies to decide certain legal matters, used differently in England, France, and the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation between political penalties (removal from office) and criminal penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: In America...when they have deprived the offender of his official rank, and have declared him incapable of filling any political office for the future, their jurisdiction terminates and that of the ordinary tribunals begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville sets a design principle: political proceedings should primarily produce administrative sanctions (removal, disqualification), while ordinary courts should apply criminal punishments (liberty, life). This limits political tribunals' severity compared with European practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction as an administrative sanctioning mechanism rather than a criminal court
rubrics_metrics.description: The main object of the political jurisdiction which obtains in the United States is, therefore, to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again. This is evidently an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville emphasizes that political trials in America are crafted to be administrative in effect—focused on removal and future ineligibility—though wrapped in judicial forms, which shapes their purpose and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad or vague descriptions of political offences increase majority power and risk abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Article II...‘The President, Vice-President, and all civil officers of the United States shall be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.’ Many of the Constitutions of the States are even less explicit...some constitutions no offences are specified, in order to subject the public functionaries to an unlimited responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that vague textual formulations (e.g., ‘other high crimes and misdemeanors,’ ‘misconduct or maladministration’) combined with mild penalties make political sanctions easier and more certain to apply, thereby strengthening majoritarian control and risking abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mildness of political penalties makes them socially severe and an effective instrument of majority control
rubrics_metrics.description: To condemn a political opponent to death...is horrible; but to declare that opponent unworthy to exercise that authority, to deprive him of it, and to leave him uninjured in life and limb, may be judged to be the fair issue of the struggle...it destroys their position in the world, casts a blight upon their honor, and condemns them to a shameful inactivity worse than death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although formal penalties may be less severe, their social and career consequences are devastating; designers of institutions should account for non-legal harms produced by administrative sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism principle: enumerated federal powers, residual powers to states
rubrics_metrics.description: The attributes of the Federal Government were therefore carefully enumerated and all that was not included amongst them was declared to constitute a part of the privileges of the several Governments of the States. Thus the government of the States remained the rule, and that of the Confederation became the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design principle: assign a limited set of general/external functions to the national government and leave internal, numerous, and indefinite matters to states. Tocqueville frames this as a deliberate way to preserve states' primacy except where union-wide action is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a high federal court to maintain balance between Union and States
rubrics_metrics.description: A high Federal court was created...which was destined, amongst other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the Constitution between the two rival Governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville recommends a specialized federal tribunal (supreme court) to resolve conflicts about limits of federal authority and to protect the constitutional division of powers; its action is indirect and intended to avoid leaving such questions to state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning external relations and select general internal functions to the federal government
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was granted to the Union...The Union was invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads which were to establish a communication between the different parts of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guideline: allocate matters requiring unified direction (war, diplomacy, currency, national infrastructure, postal system, general taxation) to the federal level, while allowing states independence in the ordinary internal ordering of society; federal interference in states permitted only in a few predetermined cases to protect the Union.
